Ledgers reports/mutation/probe-splitPointers-{m1,m6,m5,m2,selfgate}.jsonl. Parse-level: 0 differing pointer arrays out of 1 410 designed cells and 0 out of 40 000 fuzzed cells.
verdicts.argument: The mutant seeds the chunk accumulator with the constant string `Stryker was here`. `splitPointers` has exactly one consumer in the tree — the `for (const chunk of splitPointers(segment))` loop in `parseEvidencePointers` — and the only way a chunk becomes anything is `chunk.trim().match(POINTER_PREFIX)` with `POINTER_PREFIX = /\b(file|test|adr):(\S.*)$/`, which requires the literal text `file:`, `test:` or `adr:`. The injected string contains no `:` character at all, so it cannot match, and a chunk that does not match is skipped by `continue` — it contributes nothing. The element is prepended, so every chunk cut from the operator's segment is byte-identical to the pristine one; the returned array differs by one inert element and the pointer array, which is all any caller ever sees, is identical for EVERY possible input. A mission can only supply a cell, and the cell's parse does not move.

verdicts.argument: The mutant makes the FIRST chunk carry the prefix `Stryker was here!`. Every path by which that could move a pointer is closed. (1) It cannot CREATE one: the literal has no `:`, and `POINTER_PREFIX` needs `file:`, `test:` or `adr:`. (2) It cannot DESTROY one: the pattern is unanchored at the front, so text before the pointer is skipped, and its `\b` still holds because the literal's last character is `!`, a non-word character, so the transition to the `f` of `file:` is a word boundary in the mutant exactly as at the start of a string in the baseline. (3) It cannot MOVE a cut: unlike the segment-level prefix, this one is written into `buf`, never into `segment`, and every cut decision is `/(^|[\s,])(file|test|adr):\S/.test(segment.slice(i))` over the untouched `segment` — so the chunk BOUNDARIES are bit-for-bit those of the baseline and only the content of the first chunk gains the prefix. (4) The `out.filter((x) => x.trim())` at the end cannot be turned by it either: a first chunk that used to be `""` and was dropped now reads `Stryker was here!` and is kept, but the consumer immediately does `chunk.trim().match(POINTER_PREFIX)` on it, which is `null`. No pointer, no field, no count can differ for any cell.

Ledgers reports/mutation/probe-splitPointers-{m1,m6,m5,m2,selfgate}.jsonl. Parse-level: 0 differing pointer arrays over 1 410 designed and 40 000 fuzzed cells.
verdicts.argument: The mutant deletes the `^` alternative, and that alternative is unreachable code at this call site. The regex is only ever evaluated as the right-hand operand of `if (/\s|,/.test(ch) && /(^|[\s,])(file|test|adr):\S/.test(segment.slice(i)))`, with `ch === segment[i]`. `&&` short-circuits, so the regex runs only when `/\s|,/.test(ch)` is true — that is, only when `segment[i]` is a whitespace character or a comma. Its subject is `segment.slice(i)`, whose character 0 IS that same `segment[i]`. The `^` branch matches the empty string at index 0 and then requires `file`, `test` or `adr` at index 0; index 0 holds a whitespace character or a comma, so that branch can never succeed. `^` without the `m` flag matches nowhere else. Every match the original can find therefore goes through the `[\s,]` branch, which the mutant keeps unchanged, and the two patterns return the same `.test()` result on every subject this call site can construct. The mutated capture group is never read — the call is `.test`, not `.match`. No cell, and therefore no mission, can distinguish them.

verdicts.argument: Same mechanism as the line-66 mutant, applied to every chunk after a cut rather than to the first: the buffer restarts with `Stryker was here!` instead of empty. The closures are identical and none of them depends on which chunk it is. (1) The literal has no `:`, so it cannot make `POINTER_PREFIX = /\b(file|test|adr):(\S.*)$/` match where it did not. (2) The pattern is unanchored at the front and the literal ends in `!`, a non-word character, so the `\b` before `file:`/`test:`/`adr:` still holds and no pointer is lost. (3) The prefix is written into `buf`, never into `segment`, so the cut decisions — all of the form `test(segment.slice(i))` over an untouched string — are bit-for-bit the baseline's; the chunks are the same, one constant longer at the head. (4) The trailing `filter` can only be turned in the harmless direction: a chunk that was `""` becomes `Stryker was here!` and survives, but the consumer's `chunk.trim().match(POINTER_PREFIX)` on it is `null`. The `raw` field the operator reads in a violation is rebuilt from what the regex captured after `file:`/`test:`/`adr:`, never from the head of the chunk, so even the printed sentence cannot move — which the byte-identical payloads confirm.

verdicts.argument: Removing the filter changes exactly which chunks reach the consumer, and the chunks it removes are precisely those on which the consumer is a no-op. `out.filter((x) => x.trim())` drops a chunk if and only if `x.trim()` is falsy, and for a string that means `x.trim() === ""` — the chunk is empty or entirely whitespace (JavaScript's `trim` strips exactly the WhiteSpace and LineTerminator set, so a chunk made only of spaces, TAB, CR, U+2028, U+2029, NBSP or BOM trims to `""`). The sole consumer's first act on each chunk is `chunk.trim().match(POINTER_PREFIX)`, i.e. it matches against that same `""`, and `POINTER_PREFIX = /\b(file|test|adr):(\S.*)$/` requires the literal text `file:`, `test:` or `adr:` — which the empty string cannot contain. A chunk the filter would have dropped therefore yields `null`, hits the `continue`, and produces nothing. Keeping it costs one loop iteration and changes no pointer, no field and no count, for any cell whatsoever.

verdicts.argument: The predicate becomes the truthiness of the raw chunk instead of the truthiness of its trimmed form. For strings those two predicates disagree on exactly one class of value: the whitespace-only chunk, which is truthy as `x` but falsy as `x.trim()` — the empty string is falsy under both. So the mutant differs from the original only by keeping whitespace-only chunks that the original dropped. Those chunks are inert for the same reason as the sibling mutant: the only consumer immediately evaluates `chunk.trim().match(POINTER_PREFIX)`, a whitespace-only chunk trims to `""`, and `POINTER_PREFIX = /\b(file|test|adr):(\S.*)$/` cannot match a string that does not contain `file:`, `test:` or `adr:`. The chunk is skipped by `continue` and produces no pointer. Nothing downstream counts chunks — the pointer array is the function's whole observable effect — so no mission can distinguish the two predicates.
